Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
You can never know who will harm you

vignette: At fifty-nine, Elena Reyes had spent four days in a windowless holding cell after her abduction. The guards barred a heavy steel door from the outside, ensuring she had absolutely no exit. For those ninety-six hours, the only movement she was permitted was a rigid, forward-leaning posture that left her cervical muscles locked in a persistent, grinding ache. When she was finally released, the physical bruises faded, but the psychological architecture shifted permanently. She returned to her job as a project manager in Chicago, but the memory of that sealed room never healed; instead, it laid the groundwork for a new way of navigating the world. Within months, the past began to bleed into her present. Whenever the familiar band of tension tightened around her cervical muscles, or whenever a heavy door clicked shut, her body automatically shifted into high gear. These physical cues didn't just ache; they ignited a state of constant vigilance, ensuring she remained on guard and completely unable to relax, while her nervous system routinely misfired false alarms even in quiet rooms. The relentless intrusion of these confined spaces and unyielding neck pain also reshaped how she viewed her own psychology. Elena had come to believe that her capacity for joy had been permanently severed, convinced that she could never know who would harm her again. Her baseline mood plummeted into a deep, untroubled flatness, leaving her feeling dead inside and watching her former social circle drift away. Because she was certain she was fundamentally broken and perpetually unsafe, her threat monitoring never deactivated. The fear of harm and the conviction that she had lost her happiness acted as a permanent amplifier for her hypervigilance, keeping her false alarms firing and preventing any genuine unwinding. This negative self-perception actively sharpened her environmental scanning. Her deep-seated belief that she was miserable and vulnerable turned her attention toward confinement, pulling her focus directly toward locked spaces and the sensation of having no options. Her constant false alarms and inability to relax kept her nervous system primed, which in turn magnified her perception of everyday cues, making ordinary doorways feel like death traps. The sheer exhaustion of living in a state of perpetual alertness forced her into rigid cognitive coping mechanisms. To manage the relentless sense of danger and her inability to relax, Elena began telling herself that the abduction had never truly been that catastrophic, and when anxiety spiked, she retreated into self-blame rumination and relentless overanalysis of the event's timeline. These mental habits only deepened the psychological chasm. The more Elena clung to magical thinking and forced herself to overanalyse the past, the more convinced she became that her emotional numbness was permanent. Dedicating her cognitive energy to self-blame reinforced her negative appraisal that she was fundamentally unhappy and unsafe. Meanwhile, her relentless overanalysis and self-blame rumination kept her threat system locked in overdrive, ensuring her hypervigilance never deactivated and her false alarms continued to fire without pause. This loop became inescapable in her professional life. During a quarterly budget review in a high-rise conference room, the automatic lock engaged with a heavy thud. The sound alone triggered a wave of paralysis; the sudden realization that she was in a locked space mirrored that original confinement exactly. Her neck seized with familiar pain, and because she was certain that harm could arrive without warning, she stood up abruptly, knocking her coffee cup to the floor. She couldn't relax, her pulse hammering, convinced that a false alarm was actually a real threat. Instead of stepping out, she retreated into magical thinking, insisting to herself that nothing could possibly go wrong here, and then immediately spiraled into self-blame rumination for losing control. This cycle cost her two promotions. Her team grew frustrated with her abrupt departures and intense focus on room configurations, and she quietly resigned her project lead role six months ago. Elena finally walked into the clinic on a rain-swept Tuesday. She was hoping to understand why her body still treated every closed door as a death sentence, and what she could do to stop feeling dead inside. What frightened her most was the realization that she had spent the last decade trying to outrun a threat that never stopped following her, and that she was running out of rooms to hide in.
